name: Lingual braces
lead: Lingual braces are fixed orthodontic appliances bonded to the tongue-facing (inner) surfaces of the teeth instead of the outer surfaces. People choose them to straighten crowded or crooked teeth and correct bite problems while keeping the hardware out of sight, so the smile looks natural throughout treatment and the finished alignment improves how the teeth and smile look. [1]

The appliance uses brackets and archwires, the same basic principle as conventional braces: steady light forces move teeth into new positions. Because the brackets sit behind the teeth, they are nearly invisible from the front. Modern systems, such as 3M's Incognito, use CAD/CAM technology to make brackets and wires customised to each patient's tooth surfaces. [1] The technique was developed in the mid-1970s by the California orthodontist Craven Kurz, whose first patient wanted braces without visible metal, and whose practice was largely adults and celebrities. [1]

Wikipedia's account of the technique, drawing on a 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis, reports that lingual braces are associated with more tongue pain, harder oral hygiene and more speech and eating difficulty than labial braces, and that finishing movements are mechanically more demanding because the brackets sit closer together. [1] A separate 2017 meta-analysis of cephalometric outcomes found no statistically significant overall difference in tooth positions between labial and lingual appliances. [7]

In looksmaxxing communities, braces in general are discussed mainly in terms of whether they improve the smile or can alter facial structure; lingual braces as a separate topic appear far less often than discussion of braces overall. [2][3][8][9]

paras: Lingual braces consist of brackets and wires attached to the back of the teeth. Their principal advantage is that they are almost invisible in ordinary view, compared with brackets on the cheek-facing side. [1] Modern systems may use customised brackets made from digital scans, whereas early designs used prefabricated brackets. [1]

Placement methods have evolved. An early system called the Torque Angulation Referencing Guide let clinicians position brackets directly on the inner tooth surfaces using the natural tooth anatomy as a guide. A later service, the Custom Lingual Appliance Set-Up, let clinicians arrange brackets on a laboratory model first and transfer them to the mouth with a tray (indirect bonding), which became the approach for most lingual cases. [1]

In 1999 Neumann and Holtgrave presented the use of self-ligating brackets in lingual treatment, suggesting that SPEED labial self-ligating brackets could be applied in the lingual technique. [1] Kurz's original brackets also borrowed reciprocal tip and torque values from Lawrence Andrews' Straightwire Appliance, with first-order bends placed in the wires because the brackets did not carry them. [1]

The two basic bonding routes are direct placement, where a clinician positions each bracket in the mouth, and indirect bonding, where brackets are positioned on a laboratory model of the teeth and transferred in a tray. Digital workflows now plan the same positions on scanned models, and some systems have wires bent by robot to match the planned arch. [1]

Craven Kurz, working with Jim Mulick at the UCLA School of Dentistry, developed the first lingual appliance in 1975 and 1976 and treated the first patient in Beverly Hills in 1976, after the patient asked for braces without visible metal. Kurz's practice was largely adult patients, many of them celebrities. Early problems included tongue irritation, speech difficulty and a high rate of broken brackets, partly because lower teeth bit on the upper brackets. [1]

Ormco began developing lingual brackets with Kurz. Adding an inclined plane to the brackets, which converted shearing forces into compressive forces, lowered failure rates, and Kurz filed a patent in 1976. Ormco produced the first brackets in 1979 and went on to make seven generations of brackets with Kurz through the late 1980s, adding hooks, torque values and a transpalatal bar hook. [1]

In the early 1980s other companies such as Unitek and Forestadent started their own lingual research groups, and Kurz lectured to orthodontists across the United States. Professional societies for lingual orthodontics formed in France in 1986 and later in the United States, Europe and the United Kingdom, up to 2003. [1]

Interest declined around 1989 after clinicians reported difficulties and returned from about 2008 as laboratory techniques and digital technology improved. [1] Dirk Wiechmann's Incognito system, made by 3M in Germany, was reported in 2003 in the American Journal of Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopedics after testing on 600 bonded arches in his private practice over 18 months. [1]

Professional societies followed the clinical interest. The Societe Francaise d'Orthodontie Linguale formed in 1986, the American Lingual Orthodontic Association in 1987 and the European Society of Lingual Orthodontics in 1992, with the British Lingual Orthodontic Society following in 2003. In 2005 Asif Chatoo opened the London Lingual Orthodontic Clinic, described as the first UK practice dedicated to lingual orthodontics. [1]

Ormco's lingual brackets went through seven generations between 1976 and the late 1980s. The first (1976) was a low-profile bracket without hooks; hooks on canines came in 1980 and on premolars and front brackets in 1982; later generations lowered the front inclined plane, raised torque values for the upper incisors (1985), added transpalatal bar hooks on molars (1988) and finally introduced a heart-shaped inclined plane and longer hooks for elastic ligation. [1]

Several manufacturers make lingual systems. Wikipedia lists Incognito (3M), ALIAS and Stb Light (Ormco), Innovation L (Dentsply/GAC International), eBrace (Riton BioMaterials) and Harmony (American Orthodontics). [1]

Incognito uses CAD/CAM so that bracket fabrication and positioning are planned on computer models, and brackets and wires are customised to each patient's inner tooth surface. Its bracket bases are larger than some others but thinner and use less bonding material; the low profile may reduce tongue irritation but requires first-order bends in the wires. [1]

Lingual brackets sit closer to the centre of resistance of the tooth than labial brackets do, so biting forces pass through the front teeth in a way that may produce slight intrusion of the upper front teeth. The forces involved are small, in milligrams, while an optimum intrusion force is cited as 30 to 40 grams. [1]

Lower teeth biting on the upper brackets create a bite-plane effect that can help correct deep bite, but may open the bite at the back and, according to the account, can worsen a Class II relationship as the lower jaw rotates down and back. [1]

The distance between front brackets is about 40 percent smaller than with labial braces, so compensating bends and space-closing loops are harder to make. Lingual treatment can also show vertical and horizontal bowing of the arch during space closure, which clinicians counter with anti-bowing curves, lighter retraction forces or steel ligation of back teeth. [1]

Reported advantages are appearance during treatment and fewer visible decalcification marks on the outer tooth surfaces, although poor hygiene can still produce white spot lesions on the cheek-facing sides. [1]

Reported disadvantages include tongue irritation, speech difficulty and a higher rate of bracket breakage, particularly with earlier designs. Manufacturers made brackets smaller and smoother over the years, and patients are typically told irritation and speech effects improve over two to three weeks. [1]

A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis by Ata-Ali and colleagues in the American Journal of Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopedics found more tongue pain, harder oral hygiene and more speech and eating difficulty with lingual braces than with labial braces. [1]

A 2005 study by Stamm, Hohoff and Ehmer compared prefabricated Ormco brackets with customised Incognito brackets in 40 German-speaking women and reported fewer long-term tongue-space restrictions, pressure sores and reddening or lesions with the customised brackets; its measures rested on patients' own reports. [1]

A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis in BMC Oral Health compared labial and lingual fixed appliances. It searched PubMed-Medline, the Cochrane Library and LILACS through April 2017 and included four studies with 249 patients. Of six cephalometric angles and distances, lingual appliances showed non-significant trends toward a larger interincisal angle and a smaller angle between the upper central incisor and the sella-nasion plane; the authors concluded that lingual appliances appear to favour incisor tipping through lingual crown torque but that values did not differ overall, and called for standardised measurements. [7]

Among broader orthodontic research, a randomised trial of 66 adults (32 with Invisalign aligners, 34 with fixed appliances) compared finished case quality; it did not test lingual braces. [4] No randomised trial of lingual braces as a facial-aesthetic treatment has been published.

Forum threads about braces mostly ask whether they improve looks, whether they suit a slight overbite, and whether treatments with extractions or rubber bands change the face. One poster asks whether Damon braces or other types are better. [2] A teenager asks whether braces cause facial recession after seeing TikTok videos making that claim, and a reply says braces done correctly are fine and that the poster should not worry. [3] Other thread titles describe braces recessing or narrowing the face, ask about braces with tooth removal or elastic bands, and offer a guide to 'best options' before getting braces. [5][6][9][10][11]

Lingual braces as a distinct topic are discussed less often than metal braces or clear aligners; the clinical literature describes their near invisibility from the front as the main appeal, and the specialist orthodontic skills they require as a limit on availability. [1][2][9]

lore.intro: Community discussion concerns braces generally, rather than lingual braces specifically, and centres on facial change. [2][3]

claims.claim: Braces, especially with extractions or rubber bands, can recess the face or narrow it
claims.believers: Posters cite TikTok videos and personal worry that braces prevent the upper and lower jaws from growing properly, and threads describe braces that 'recessed' the face. [3][5]
claims.experts: Orthodontic research on jaw position has mostly examined functional appliances and Class II correction rather than whether ordinary braces recess the face; no trial tested lingual braces for this outcome.

claims.claim: Braces improve how a person looks
claims.believers: A poster relays friends saying braces make a person look better and asks about fixing a slight overbite. [2]
claims.experts: Orthodontic trials measure tooth alignment and occlusal quality, as in an adult trial comparing aligners with fixed braces, rather than attractiveness ratings. [4]

card.summary: Braces bonded behind the teeth to hide them; discreet, but linked to more tongue and speech trouble than outer braces.
card.note: Evidence concerns tooth alignment, not facial structure; reviews report more tongue pain and speech difficulty.

quick.overview:
Lingual braces are fixed braces attached to the tongue side of the teeth, so they are hard to see. They were first developed in California in the mid-1970s.

They are used to straighten teeth and correct bites. Forum discussion is mostly about braces in general and whether they change facial structure, a question with little direct research.
quick.mechanism: Brackets and wires on the inner tooth surfaces apply steady forces that move teeth, the same principle as braces on the outer surfaces.
quick.risks: A 2016 review summarised in encyclopedic sources reports more tongue pain, speech and eating difficulty and harder cleaning than with outer braces; brackets break more often in some designs. White spot lesions can still occur with poor hygiene. Treatment is delivered by orthodontists.

chain: Brackets bonded to the inner tooth surfaces
Wires move teeth into alignment over months
Straighter teeth and a corrected bite, with nothing visible from the front during treatment
angle.text: Lingual braces straighten teeth the way other braces do, and their placement behind the teeth lets people keep a natural-looking smile throughout treatment. Users who want aligned teeth without visible metal, including adults in public-facing roles, are the group the appliance was originally designed for. [1]
